R e s u l t s
Clinical Features of PERM Patients

cases.text:
Patient 1
A 54-year-old man presented in October 2006 with
subacute onset of difficulty walking and profuse sweating.
Neurological examination showed restricted upward
gaze, axial rigidity with leg spasms and brisk tendon re-
flexes in all limbs [modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 3]. His
cranial and spinal MRI examinations were normal and
CSF examination showed 7 lymphocytes, increased pro-
tein (71 mg/dl), normal glucose concentration, oligoclo-
nal IgG bands (pattern 3), increased IgG index (1.1) and
no malignant cells. Electromyography (EMG) demon-

strated involuntary continuous motor unit activity. In the
following years, his clinical findings slowly progressed
and at his final visit (October 2011), in addition to gener-
alized stiffness, rigidity and upward gaze restriction, he
had right central facial palsy, spastic paraparesis, myo-
clonic jerks and startle response elicited by light touch
(mRS 5). Cranial and spinal MRI scans were normal and
a second CSF analysis yielded inflammatory findings sim-
ilar to the first analysis. An 18-fluoro-deoxy-glucose (18-
FDG) PET scan showed hypermetabolism in the left me-
dial temporal lobe, putamen and insula and an EEG ex-
amination showed slow waves and epileptiform discharg-
es in the left hemisphere. No clinical seizure manifestation
was observed or reported by the patient. Routine com-
plete blood count, biochemical analysis, serum B12 levels,
thyroid function tests, serology for HIV1 and HTLV1 and
annual screenings for tumors and vasculitic-rheumato-
logic diseases were normal or negative. Although non-
immunological diagnostic options were considered, late
onset and subacute presentation of the symptoms, plus
absence of family history and inflammatory CSF findings
suggested an underlying autoimmune mechanism
prompting immunotherapy. However, the patient did
not respond to 7 pulse steroid and intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIg) treatment courses performed on several
occasions between November 2006 and December 2011
and did not give consent for any other treatments.

Patient 2
A 46-year-old man presented with diplopia, dysphagia
and gait ataxia. Within 3 months, he progressed to have
generalized stiffness, rigidity, myoclonus and tactile stim-
ulus-induced startle response. Neurological examination
showed mild paresis of the right abducens nerve, bilat-
eral cerebellar findings, rigidity, stiffness, myoclonic jerks
and brisk tendon reflexes (mRS 4). CSF examination
showed 12 lymphocytes, increased protein (62 mg/dl),
normal glucose, increased IgG index (1.4) and no malig-
nant cells. EMG showed involuntary continuous motor
unit activity. Complete blood count and biochemical
analysis, CSF OCB, EEG, cranial/spinal MRI, brain 18-
FDG PET and a screening for vasculitic-rheumatologic
diseases were normal or negative. A contrast-enhanced
whole-body CT showed a left renal mass, and pathologi-
cal examination of the tissue revealed renal cell carcino-
ma. Following pulse steroid treatment (5 × 1 g i.v. meth-
ylprednisolone) and left nephrectomy, his brainstem,
cerebellar symptoms and rigidity significantly regressed,
and myoclonic jerks and the startle response disappeared.
However, due to residual cerebellar symptoms and rigid-
ity, his mRS remained at 3 in a follow-up period of 2 years
under azathioprine treatment.

Patient 3
This 67-year-old man was admitted with subacute on-
set of amnesia followed by left focal motor seizures.
Within 2 months, he gradually developed generalized ri-
gidity, stiffness, myoclonic jerks, dysphagia and mutism
followed by stupor. Neurological examination displayed
brisk tendon reflexes and extensor plantar responses
(mRS 5). CSF examination showed 18 lymphocytes, in-
creased protein (57 mg/dl), normal glucose, increased
IgG index (0.9), but no oligoclonal IgG bands. EMG re-
vealed involuntary continuous motor unit activity. While
his cranial and spinal MRI scans and EEG were normal,
18-FDG PET showed hypermetabolism in the right me-
dial temporal lobe. Complete blood count test, biochem-
ical analysis and extensive tumor and vasculitic-rheuma-
tologic disease screenings were unremarkable. The pa-
tient responded favorably to anticonvulsants, pulse
steroid (5 × 1 g i.v. methylprednisolone) and IVIg (2 g/
kg every 4 weeks) treatments. Five months after the onset
of the symptoms, his neurological examination was nor-
mal except mild residual amnesia (mRS 1). He has not
developed new symptoms in a follow-up period of 3
years.
The diagnosis of PERM was established in all 3 pa-
tients based on the core symptoms of generalized rigidity,
stiffness, myoclonic jerks, additional central nervous sys-
tem (CNS) findings, inflammatory CSF findings and in-
voluntary continuous motor unit activity in EMG exami-
nations. While all patients displayed brainstem and/or
cerebellar system dysfunction, patients 1 and 3 also had
symptoms consistent with cortical and/or subcortical
CNS involvement. Despite severe neurological symp-
toms, MRI scans were normal in all patients. However,
patients 1 and 2 showed pathological features in PET and/
or EEG examinations suggesting supratentorial cortico-
subcortical involvement ( table 1 ). All 3 patients had clin-
ical and paraclinical features suggestive of possible neu-
ronal antibody associated syndrome
[15] , prompting the
investigation of an extensive panel of antineuronal anti-
bodies.
Antineuronal Antibodies in PERM Patients
Patients 1 and 2 did not have serum antibodies to any
of the well-characterized antineuronal antibodies associ-
ated with paraneoplastic encephalopathies or PERM. By
contrast, patient 3 showed antibodies directed against the
VGKC-complex and GAD. Further analysis of his serum

tibodies ( table 2 ). Notably, he was the only patient who
significantly responded to immunotherapy ( table 1 ).
Due to the absence of a well-characterized antineuro-
nal autoantibody, the serum sample of patient 2 was
screened with protein macroarray for identification of
novel antineuronal antibodies. Only the clone that yield-
ed the highest signal intensity (score 3), paraneoplastic
antigen Ma3 (accession number, NM_013364; molecular
weight, 52 kDa), was further studied. Sequencing studies
demonstrated a single clone that matched the Ma3 pro-
tein. SDS-PAGE analysis of the purified protein showed
a single band at ∼ 50 kDa, as predicted. ELISA studies
showed high-titer Ma3 antibodies only in patient 2 but
not in other PERM patients, control MS patients or
healthy individuals ( table 2 , fig. 1 ). None of the sera re-
acted with an irrelevant protein (zinc finger protein 335)
purified from the E. coli strain also used to express Ma3
and the lysate of the same E. coli strain with no human
protein expression (data not shown).
Discussion
PERM patients may present with diverse clinical fea-
tures, tumor types and antibody responses. While most
previous cases of PERM were associated with GAD anti-
bodies (60–80%)
[1, 6] , some PERM patients with or

without a tumor have recently been shown to display an-
tibodies to GlyR, amphiphysin and other neuronal anti-
gens
[2, 3, 8, 9] and several seronegative patients have also
been reported [1, 10] . In resemblance to the reported cas-
es, the clinical features and antibody responses of our
small cohort showed a great variety. This variety included
the duration of the clinical progression (years in patient
1 vs. months in patients 2 and 3). Likewise, the duration
of PERM in reported cases has ranged from weeks to sev-
eral years
[1] . The heterogeneity of the immunological
and clinical features suggests that PERM is caused by di-
verse pathogenic mechanisms that mainly afflict the spi-
nal cord and brainstem and less frequently discrete supra-
tentorial CNS regions.
While the exact pathogenic mechanisms of PERM
symptoms remain obscure in patients 1 and 2, they are
presumably induced by antineuronal antibodies in pa-
tient 3. This patient clearly represents the so-called neu-
ronal surface antibody syndrome, which is characterized
by serum/CSF antibodies against neuronal surface anti-
gens, possible antibody-mediated pathogenesis and good
response to immunomodulatory therapies
[15] . Similar
to a recently reported PERM case with GlyR and NMDAR
antibodies
[9] , patient 3 presented with antibodies to 2
different synapse antigens, LGI1 and GAD. In both pa-
tients, the atypical limbic symptoms of seizures and am-
nesia may plausibly be attributed to the coexistence of an
ion channel-associated antibody, particularly the LGI1
and NMDAR antibodies. Moreover, myoclonic jerks
have been reported in up to 40% of patients with LGI1-Ab
[16] , and rigidity spasms, epileptic in origin, are not un-
common in LGI-Ab encephalitis [17] , further supporting
that the symptomatology of patient 3 might be explained
by combined effects of immunities to LGI1 (causing lim-
bic encephalitis) and GAD (causing SPS). Nevertheless,
PERM patients without well-characterized ion channel
antibodies such as our patient 1 and some of the previ-
ously reported cases
[8] have also displayed clinical or
EEG seizures and cortical involvement, indicating the
presence of additional factors causing epileptic phenom-
ena in PERM.
Ma3 antibodies have been shown in several autoim-
mune encephalitis cases, generally in coexistence with
Ma2 antibodies and a tumor
[18] . Protein macroarray
and ELISA results of our study introduce Ma3 as a novel
PERM-associated autoantigen and add a new syndrome
to the spectrum of Ma3 antibody-associated neurological
diseases. It is well known that patients with Ma immu-
nity may develop rigidity of extrapyramidal origin be-
cause of upper brainstem encephalitis. Actually, some of
the clinical features of patient 2 overlap with the seminal
description of encephalitis with immunity to Ma proteins
and may be attributed to Ma3 immunity
[18] .
The MRI scans of our patients were normal, as were
those of most reported PERM patients with or without
supratentorial involvement
[3, 7, 8] . However, PET ex-
aminations of 2 patients revealed abnormal signals in sev-
eral supratentorial regions, suggesting that PET is a more
sensitive tool in diagnosing the pathological CNS altera-
tions in PERM. Nevertheless, even PET studies failed to
show pathological findings at the spinal cord, brainstem
and cerebellum, suggesting that different pathological
processes are in play in infratentorial and supratentorial
CNS regions of PERM patients.
There appear to be no prominent clinical differences
between seronegative versus seropositive or paraneoplas-
tic versus non-paraneoplastic PERM cases (
[1, 7–10] and
our patients). Also, PERM patients with different anti-
bodies present with similar clinical features. For example,
seizures and cognitive dysfunction that have been mainly
observed in association with GlyR antibodies
[3] were
also observed in our patients with no GlyR antibodies.
However, our patient 3 with antibodies to neuronal sur-
face antigens showed the most significant amelioration
following immunotherapy. Thus, detection of a neuronal
surface antibody in a PERM patient might be a marker for
favorable response to treatment, as it is in several other
autoimmune encephalopathies
[15, 19] .
In conclusion, our findings indicate that PERM is a
syndrome generated by diverse pathogenic mechanisms,

CNS regions. These mechanisms might include humoral
responses inducing pathogenic antibodies to cell surface
antigens causing neuronal surface antibody syndrome
[15] , as well as antibodies to intracellular antigens pend-
ing to be characterized. It is rather difficult to distinguish
distinct PERM immunophenotypes based on clinical
findings. The antibody tests should nevertheless be per-
formed for identification of treatment-resistant and
treatment-responsive patients.
